claim: Biofilms are complex agglomerations of sessile, microbial cells surrounded in a self-secreted extracellular matrix that is composed primarily of exopolysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids.
source: Biofilms are complex agglomerations of sessile, microbial cells surrounded in a self-secreted extracellular matrix that is composed primarily of exopolysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004, which provides external scholarly support for the definition of biofilms.

claim: Biofilm-forming pathogenic bacteria have been associated with numerous persistent and nosocomial infections in humans, such as infection of the ear or urinary tract or colonizing the lungs of patients suffering from cystic fibrosis.
source: Biofilm-forming pathogenic bacteria have been associated with numerous persistent and nosocomial infections in humans, such as infection of the ear or urinary tract or colonizing the lungs of patients suffering from cystic fibriosis (Parsek and Singh, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parsek and Singh, 2003, which provides external scholarly support for the association between biofilm-forming bacteria and human infections.

claim: Bacteria in biofilms can withstand antibiotic treatment, making many clinically relevant antibiotics ineffective in the treatment of biofilm-related bacterial infections.
source: Because bacteria in biofilms can withstand antibiotic treatment, many clinically relevant antibiotics are ineffective in the treatment of biofilm-related bacterial infections (Mah and O'Toole, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mah and O'Toole, 2001, which provides external scholarly support for the antibiotic tolerance of biofilm bacteria.

claim: The decision to transition between a planktonic and a biofilm life-style is orchestrated by the near ubiquitous bacterial second messenger cyclic-di-GMP (c-di-GMP).
source: The decision to transition between a planktonic and a biofilm life-style is orchestrated by the near ubiquitous bacterial second messenger cyclic-di-GMP (c-di-GMP), a dinucleotide known to modulate many different aspects of bacterial physiology (Ross et al., 1987; Hengge, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ross et al., 1987 and Hengge, 2009, which provide external scholarly support for the role of c-di-GMP in bacterial physiology.

claim: The dinucleotide c-di-GMP is synthesized from two molecules of GTP by diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) containing a GGDEF domain.
source: The dinucleotide is synthesized from two molecules of GTP by diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) containing a GGDEF domain, and hydrolyzed by phosphodiesterases (PDEs) with either an EAL or a HD-GYP domain (Tal et al., 1998; Simm et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2006; Schirmer and Jenal, 2009; Krasteva et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Tal et al., 1998; Simm et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2006; Schirmer and Jenal, 2009; Krasteva et al., 2012) that provide external scholarly support for the synthesis of c-di-GMP.

claim: C-di-GMP is hydrolyzed by phosphodiesterases (PDEs) with either an EAL or a HD-GYP domain.
source: The dinucleotide is synthesized from two molecules of GTP by diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) containing a GGDEF domain, and hydrolyzed by phosphodiesterases (PDEs) with either an EAL or a HD-GYP domain (Tal et al., 1998; Simm et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2006; Schirmer and Jenal, 2009; Krasteva et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Tal et al., 1998; Simm et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2006; Schirmer and Jenal, 2009; Krasteva et al., 2012) that provide external scholarly support for the hydrolysis of c-di-GMP.

claim: In Pseudomonas fluorescens, biofilm formation is dependent on a signaling protein referred to as LapD.
source: In Pseudomonas fluorescens, biofilm formation is dependent on such a signaling protein, referred to as LapD (Hinsa and O'Toole, 2006; Newell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hinsa and O'Toole, 2006 and Newell et al., 2009, which provide external scholarly support for the role of LapD in P. fluorescens biofilm formation.

claim: LapD is a transmembrane receptor that contains a cytoplasmic GGDEF–EAL domain module that lacks enzymatic activity, though the EAL domain has retained its capacity to bind c-di-GMP.
source: This transmembrane receptor contains a cytoplasmic GGDEF–EAL domain module that lacks enzymatic activity, though the EAL domain has retained its capacity to bind c-di-GMP.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript text and describes the structural and functional properties of LapD.

claim: Cytosolic c-di-GMP levels in P. fluorescens are regulated in response to nutrient availability, specifically the amount of inorganic phosphate.
source: Cytosolic c-di-GMP levels in P. fluorescens are regulated in response to nutrient availability, specifically the amount of inorganic phosphate (Figure 1A; Monds et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Monds et al., 2007 and reference to Figure 1A, which provides both external scholarly support and visual representation of the regulatory mechanism.

claim: Limiting phosphate increases the expression of a PDE, which lowers intracellular c-di-GMP levels, ultimately resulting in the dispersion of P. fluorescens biofilms.
source: Limiting phosphate increases the expression of a PDE, which lowers intracellular c-di-GMP levels, ultimately resulting in the dispersion of P. fluorescens biofilms.
evidence: This claim describes a mechanistic pathway linking phosphate availability to biofilm dispersal through c-di-GMP regulation.

claim: When environmental phosphate levels are high, multiple DGCs contribute to high intracellular c-di-GMP levels, resulting in stable cell attachment and subsequently biofilm formation.
source: Conversely, when environmental phosphate levels are high, multiple DGCs contribute to high intracellular c-di-GMP levels, resulting in stable cell attachment and subsequently biofilm formation (Newell et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Newell et al., 2011b, which provides external scholarly support for the relationship between phosphate, c-di-GMP, and biofilm formation.

claim: C-di-GMP-bound LapD engages the periplasmic protease LapG through its Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS)-like domain, preventing it from cleaving the cell surface-bound large adhesin LapA.
source: Specifically, c-di-GMP-bound LapD engages the periplasmic protease LapG through its Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS)-like domain, preventing it from cleaving the cell surface-bound large adhesin LapA, a protein mediating cell adhesion to multiple substrates (Navarro et al., 2011; Newell et al., 2011a; El-Kirat-Chatel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Navarro et al., 2011; Newell et al., 2011a; El-Kirat-Chatel et al., 2014) that provide external scholarly support for the mechanism of LapD-LapG interaction.

claim: C-di-GMP-unbound LapD adopts an autoinhibited conformation and loses its affinity for LapG.
source: In contrast, c-di-GMP-unbound LapD adopts an autoinhibited conformation and loses its affinity for LapG.
evidence: This claim describes the conformational state of LapD in the absence of c-di-GMP and its functional consequence.

claim: LapG accesses and cleaves LapA's N-terminus when LapD is in its autoinhibited state, releasing the bulk of the adhesin from the cell surface and destabilizing cell attachment.
source: LapG in turn accesses and cleaves LapA's N-terminus, releasing the bulk of the adhesin from the cell surface and destabilizing cell attachment (Boyd et al., 2012; Chatterjee et al., 2012; Boyd et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Boyd et al., 2012; Chatterjee et al., 2012; Boyd et al., 2014) that provide external scholarly support for the proteolytic activity of LapG.

claim: The structure of L. pneumophila CdgS9Output was determined from data collected on a crystal grown from selenomethionine-derivatized protein by using single anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing.
source: The structure of L. pneumophila CdgS9Output (residues of 22–152) was determined from data collected on a crystal grown from selenomethionine-derivatized protein by using single anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing (see 'Material and methods', and Table 1 for details).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used to determine the crystal structure, which is a direct observation from the study.

claim: The asymmetric unit of CdgS9Output contains one molecule, which adopts a PAS-like domain fold with the highest structural homology to CitA.
source: The asymmetric unit contains one molecule of CdgS9Output, which adopts a PAS-like domain fold with the highest structural homology to CitA (Reinelt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and a citation to Reinelt et al., 2003 for structural comparison.

claim: A potential biologically relevant dimer of CdgS9Output involves a crystallographic symmetry mate, burying 3020 Å2 surface area at the twofold symmetry axis via favorable interactions.
source: A potential biologically relevant dimer involves a crystallographic symmetry mate, burying 3020 Å2 surface area at the twofold symmetry axis via favorable interactions (estimated ΔGint = −20.2 kcal/mol) (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) (Figure 1B, bottom right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data, computational analysis (citation to Krissinel and Henrick, 2007), and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The residues at the CdgS9Output homo-dimer interface tend to be more conserved than residues outside of this region, based on an alignment of 18 putative LapD orthologs from different bacterial species.
source: The residues at the CdgS9Output homo-dimer interface tend to be more conserved than residues outside of this region, based on an alignment of 18 putative LapD orthologs from different bacterial species (Figure 1C; Navarro et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis and reference to Figure 1C, which shows conservation mapping.

claim: The protomers of CdgS9Output form a parallel dimer, with the termini lining up at one end of the complex, consistent with their connectivity to the transmembrane helices that flank the periplasmic domain.
source: The protomers form a parallel dimer, with the termini lining up at one end of the complex, consistent with their connectivity to the transmembrane helices that flank the periplasmic domain.
evidence: This claim describes the structural arrangement observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The folds of the dimer half-sites between the P. fluorescens LapDOutput and CdgS9Output are almost identical with an rmsd of 1.9 Å.
source: Although the folds of the dimer half-sites between the P. fluorescens LapDOutput and CdgS9Output are almost identical (rmsd of 1.9 Å) and the conserved GWxQ motifs, which are important for LapG binding, are positioned in identical, surface-exposed loops within each half-site, the dimer topology of the two output domain ortholog structures is substantially different (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data (rmsd calculation) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The dimer topology of the two output domain ortholog structures (P. fluorescens LapDOutput and CdgS9Output) is substantially different.
source: Although the folds of the dimer half-sites between the P. fluorescens LapDOutput and CdgS9Output are almost identical (rmsd of 1.9 Å) and the conserved GWxQ motifs, which are important for LapG binding, are positioned in identical, surface-exposed loops within each half-site, the dimer topology of the two output domain ortholog structures is substantially different (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and reference to Figure 1B showing the different topologies.

claim: CdgS9Output adopts a 'parallel' conformation as opposed to the open, V-shaped form observed in LapDOutput.
source: CdgS9Output adopts a 'parallel' conformation as opposed to the open, V-shaped form that we observed in case of LapDOutput.
evidence: This claim describes the conformational difference between the two structures based on crystallographic observations.

claim: The tryptophan residues (W125 in P. fluorescens LapD; W126 in L. pneumophila CdgS9) are farther apart in the P. fluorescens dimer than the L. pneumophila LapD ortholog (50 Å vs 35 Å between their respective Cβ positions).
source: As a consequence, the tryptophan residues (W125 in P. fluorescens LapD; W126 in L. pneumophila CdgS9) that form the distal tip of the PAS fold and appear to be a main anchor point for LapG binding (Navarro et al., 2011) are farther apart in the P. fluorescens dimer than the L. pneumophila LapD ortholog (50 Å vs 35 Å between their respective Cβ positions) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements from crystal structures and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Cross-linking data indicate that the topology observed in the CdgS9Output structure represents the biologically relevant model, which is conserved in the two LapD orthologs, LapD and CdgS9.
source: Taken together, the cross-linking data clearly indicate that the topology observed in the CdgS9Output structure represents the biologically relevant model, which is conserved in the two LapD orthologs, LapD and CdgS9, despite only moderate overall sequence conservation (31% identity/52% similarity).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The two LapD orthologs, LapD and CdgS9, share only moderate overall sequence conservation (31% identity/52% similarity).
source: Taken together, the cross-linking data clearly indicate that the topology observed in the CdgS9Output structure represents the biologically relevant model, which is conserved in the two LapD orthologs, LapD and CdgS9, despite only moderate overall sequence conservation (31% identity/52% similarity).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The domain-swapped model of the P. fluorescens output domain was likely an artifact of expression and/or crystallization.
source: We suspect our previously published domain-swapped model of the P. fluorescens output domain was an artifact of expression and/or crystallization.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the cross-linking data that contradicted the previous structural model.

claim: The crystallized complex consists of two CdgS9 output domain molecules that adopt a similar parallel dimer conformation as in the apo-CdgS9Output structure.
source: The crystallized complex consists of two CdgS9 output domain molecules that adopt a similar parallel dimer conformation as in the apo-CdgS9Output structure (Figures 1B and 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and reference to Figures 1B and 3A.

claim: The output domain dimer is bound to one LapG molecule at a lateral docking site with an interaction surface of 1290 Å2.
source: The output domain dimer is bound to one LapG molecule at a lateral docking site (Figure 3A), with an interaction surface of 1290 Å2 (with a calculated ΔGint = −16.3 kcal/mol; PISA [Krissinel and Henrick, 2007]) and involving both molecules of the CdgS9Output dimer to a similar extent (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data, computational analysis, and reference to Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The conserved tryptophan residue (W126) is the major anchor point on CdgS9 as it inserts into a hydrophobic pocket at the bottom of LapG.
source: As predicted by the biochemical analysis (Navarro et al., 2011; Chatterjee et al., 2012), the aforementioned conserved tryptophan residue (W126) is the major anchor point on CdgS9 as it inserts into a hydrophobic pocket at the bottom of LapG (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and previous biochemical studies (citations to Navarro et al., 2011 and Chatterjee et al., 2012).

claim: The interface between CdgS9Output and LapG appears to be dominated by hydrophobic contacts and shape-complementarity of the interacting elements.
source: While there are contributions from a limited number of hydrogen bonds and a water-mediated interaction (Figure 3A), the interface appears to be dominated by hydrophobic contacts and shape-complementarity of the interacting elements.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the complex interface.

claim: LapG presents a cluster of conserved residues on the side that coincides with the active site and the region that interacts with CdgS9Output, while the opposite side of the protease shows poor sequence conservation.
source: Notably, there is a disparity regarding surface conservation between the two proteins: LapG presents a cluster of conserved residues on the side that coincides with the active site and the region that interacts with CdgS9Output, while the opposite side of the protease shows poor sequence conservation (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis mapped onto the structure, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CdgS9Output is less conserved overall (37% identical to P. fluorescens LapDOutput) and shows only a moderate clustering of conserved residues.
source: In contrast, CdgS9Output is less conserved overall (37% identical to P. fluorescens LapDOutput) and shows only a moderate clustering of conserved residues (Figure 3C, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The main docking site for the CdgS9–LapG interaction, the loop that contains the GW126xQ motif, is well conserved.
source: Yet, the main docking site for the CdgS9–LapG interaction, the loop that contains the GW126xQ motif, is well conserved.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The conformation of the individual output domain protomers varies only slightly in the apo and LapG-bound states (rmsd between 1.1 and 1.7 Å).
source: The conformation of the individual output domain protomers varies only slightly in the two states (rmsd between 1.1 and 1.7 Å).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data (rmsd calculation).

claim: A change in the output domain dimer interface creates a cradle that buttresses strand β4 of LapG while providing additional anchor points via the conserved GWxQ binding loop on one dimer half-side and helix α2 on the other.
source: However, from a top view a change in the output domain dimer interface is apparent (Figure 4A, left panel). As a result, a cradle is created, which buttresses strand β4 of LapG while providing additional anchor points via the conserved GWxQ binding loop on one dimer half-side and helix α2 on the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The conformational change from apo to LapG-bound state is realized through the differential packing of the central helices within the output domain dimer.
source: This conformational change is realized through the differential packing of the central helices within the output domain dimer (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and reference to Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: In the apo-state, the output domain dimer of CdgS9 contains central four-helix bundles, either via packing of helices α1 and α2 of the PAS domain fold close to the distal end, or helices α1 and α4 at the membrane-proximal region.
source: In the apo-state, the output domain dimer of CdgS9 contains central four-helix bundles, either via packing of helices α1 and α2 of the PAS domain fold close to the distal end, or helices α1 and α4 at the membrane-proximal region.
evidence: This claim describes the structural arrangement observed in the apo-state crystal structure.

claim: When engaged with LapG, the perfect symmetry between the two protomers observed in the apo-state is broken, resulting in an asymmetric complex with regard to the output domain dimer.
source: When engaged with LapG (Figures 3A and 4B), this perfect symmetry between the two protomers observed in the apo-state is broken. The resulting complex is asymmetric with regard to the output domain dimer, manifested by a 5 Å tilt and vertical offset of one PAS domain fold relative to the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and reference to Figures 3A and 4B.

claim: The isolated output domain is in a deregulated state and spontaneously populates the high-affinity conformation for LapG binding (on-state) since regulatory domains that would lock the receptor in its off-state or on-state are lacking.
source: We argue that the isolated output domain is in a deregulated state and spontaneously populates the high-affinity conformation for LapG binding (on-state) since regulatory domains that would lock the receptor in its off-state (the apo state) or on-state are lacking.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural observations and the absence of regulatory domains in the isolated construct.

claim: The isolated output domain is an inefficient competitor for the interaction between LapG and full-length LapD.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the observation that the isolated output domain is an inefficient competitor for the interaction between LapG and full-length LapD (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: P. fluorescens LapG and L. pneumophila LapG structures are very similar with regard to their overall fold (Cα rmsd of 1.09 Å over 136 atoms).
source: Despite moderate sequence conservation between the two orthologs (40% identity/54% similarity), the two structures are very similar with regard to their overall fold (Cα rmsd of 1.09 Å over 136 atoms).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data (rmsd calculation).

claim: A rare di-calcium binding motif was identified in the N-terminal lobe of P. fluorescens LapG, in contrast to the single calcium ion bound at the same site in the L. pneumophila LapG structure.
source: First, we identified a rare di-calcium binding motif in the N-terminal lobe of P. fluorescens LapG, which is in contrast to the single calcium ion bound at the same site in the L. pneumophila LapG structure (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The two LapG orthologs share the same conserved coordinating residues required for di-calcium binding.
source: Yet, the two orthologs share the same conserved coordinating residues required for di-calcium binding (Figure 5C) (Chatterjee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis and reference to Figure 5C and a citation to Chatterjee et al., 2012.

claim: A conformational change observed between CdgS9Output-bound P. fluorescens LapG and the L. pneumophila LapG ortholog localizes to the site of interaction with LapD orthologs, which involves the peeling away of β5 upon binding to LapD.
source: The second conformational change observed between CdgS9Output-bound P. fluorescens LapG and the L. pneumophila LapG ortholog localizes to the site of interaction with LapD orthologs, which involves the peeling away of β5 upon binding to LapD, whereas β5 and part of the linker are ordered in the stand-alone LapG structures (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: All the LapG variants that contained a pAzF residue at positions predicted to be close to the interaction site yielded band shifts to variable extents (V205pAzF > Y206pAzF/Y176pAzF/A169pAzF >> Y108pAzF).
source: In contrast, all the LapG variants that contained a pAzF residue at positions that, based on the structure, are predicted to be close to the interaction site yielded band shifts to variable extents (V205pAzF > Y206pAzF/Y176pAzF/A169pAzF >> Y108pAzF) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data and reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The isolated output domains of L. pneumophila CdgS9 and P. fluorescens LapD cross-link to LapG readily, suggesting that they are in a binding-competent state.
source: It is worth noting that the isolated output domains of L. pneumophila CdgS9 and P. fluorescens LapD cross-link to LapG readily, suggesting that they are in a binding-competent state, which is in agreement with our crystallographic analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data and is consistent with structural analysis.

claim: Cross-linking is more robust in the presence of c-di-GMP-activated full-length LapD protein.
source: However, cross-linking is more robust in the presence of c-di-GMP-activated full-length LapD protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data and reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The potential second binding site on the output domain dimer does not allow as tight a binding as the crystallographically determined docking site due to sub-optimal shape complementarity.
source: From this analysis, it is clear that the potential second binding site does not allow as tight a binding as the crystallographically determined docking site due to sub-optimal shape complementarity (Figure 7A, note gap indicated in bottom panel; statistic shape complementarity (Lawrence and Colman, 1993; Collaborative Computational Project N, 1994) of 0.72 for the crystallographic interface vs 0.31 for the modeled, second binding site).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling and shape complementarity calculations, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: SEC-MALS experiments show that the purified protein complex derived from co-expression elutes in a single peak with an experimentally determined average molecular weight of 56.9 kDa, consistent with a CdgS9Output dimer bound to one LapG molecule (theoretical molecular weight: 52.3 kDa).
source: The purified protein complex that was derived from co-expression of its components and yielded the native complex crystals elutes in a single peak, with an experimentally determined average molecular weight of 56.9 kDa (theoretical molecular weight for a CdgS9Output dimer bound to one LapG molecule: 52.3 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data.

claim: The homogeneous complex with both LapG and CdgS9Output from L. pneumophila yielded a single peak with a molecular weight of 50.9 kDa, consistent with a 2:1 complex.
source: We also purified the homogeneous complex with both LapG and CdgS9Output coming from L. pneumophila. This sample also yielded a single peak with a molecular weight of 50.9 kDa, consistent with a 2:1 complex (a CdgS9Output dimer bound to one LapG molecule; Figure 5B, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of an excess L. pneumophila LapG to the purified complex failed to drive the formation of a 2:2 complex.
source: More importantly, even addition of an excess L. pneumophila LapG to the purified complex failed to drive the formation of a 2:2 complex (Figure 7B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Maximum cross-linking between LapD and LapG was achieved at sub-stoichiometric LapG concentrations, roughly corresponding to a ratio of one LapG molecule per LapD dimer.
source: Strikingly, in all cases, maximum cross-linking was achieved at sub-stoichiometric LapG concentrations, roughly corresponding to a ratio of one LapG molecule per LapD dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data.

claim: No double-shift was observed at any condition, which would indicate the formation of a 2:2 complex, suggesting that this is a rather rare event.
source: No double-shift was observed at any condition, which would indicate the formation of a 2:2 complex, suggesting that this is a rather rare event.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data.

claim: The data are consistent with the formation of an asymmetric LapD–LapG complex in P. fluorescens, and this complex appears to be conserved across the two bacterial genera assessed.
source: Taken together, these experiments establish the asymmetric complex observed in the crystals as the predominant species in solution and the membrane, and this complex appears to be conserved across the two bacterial genera assessed here.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple experimental approaches including SEC-MALS and cross-linking.

claim: Increasing amounts of the MDGWMQA peptide, but not of the mutated MDGEMQA, decrease the cross-linking efficiency of Y206pAzF.
source: Here, we demonstrate that increasing amounts of the MDGWMQA peptide, but not of the mutated MDGEMQA, decrease the cross-linking efficiency of Y206pAzF (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data and reference to Figure 8A.

claim: At the highest peptide concentration, cross-linking is reduced to about 60% of the unperturbed interaction.
source: At the highest peptide concentration, cross-linking is reduced to about 60% of the unperturbed interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data.

claim: The addition of the peptide with the native sequence to LapG pull-downs from P. fluorescens lysates reduces the amount of LapD coming down with LapG, whereas the mutant peptide does not compete with the native interaction.
source: Finally, the addition of the peptide with the native sequence to LapG pull-downs from P. fluorescens lysates reduces the amount of LapD coming down with LapG, whereas the mutant peptide does not compete with the native interaction (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down experimental data and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Basal levels of cross-linking of LapG to LapD were observed in the absence of c-di-GMP in a UV-dependent manner, however addition of c-di-GMP stimulated complex formation.
source: Consistent with previous experiments, we observed basal levels of cross-linking of LapG to LapD in the absence of c-di-GMP in a UV-dependent manner, however addition of c-di-GMP stimulated complex formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data.

claim: The basal and stimulated binding is abrogated in the output domain mutants W125E and D72K, both located at the LapG binding site.
source: The basal and stimulated binding is abrogated in the output domain mutants W125E and D72K, both located at the LapG binding site, corroborating our structural model.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data on mutant proteins.

claim: S helix mutations S229D and F222E or the HAMP domain mutation I187E result in a higher basal level of LapG cross-linking, but also an elevated level of cross-linking when c-di-GMP is present.
source: S helix mutations S229D and F222E or the HAMP domain mutation I187E, which we predict to bias the HAMP domain towards an activated conformation in analogy to orthologous studies on other HAMP domain-containing proteins (Zhou et al., 2011), result in a higher basal level of LapG cross-linking, but also an elevated level of cross-linking when c-di-GMP is present (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-linking experimental data on mutant proteins and reference to Figure 9A.

claim: Wild-type LapD shows an appreciably sharp transition in LapG binding when spiked with increasing amounts of c-di-GMP, with the switch occurring between 0.75 μM and 1 μM dinucleotide.
source: Spiking wild-type LapD with increasing amounts of c-di-GMP shows an appreciably sharp transition in LapG binding, with the switch occurring between 0.75 μM and 1 μM dinucleotide.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-di-GMP titration experimental data.

claim: The mutant variants of LapD with alterations in the S helix (S229D and F222E) or the HAMP domain (I187E) show a shallower dose–response curve, in addition to higher basal levels.
source: In contrast, the mutant variants of LapD with alterations in the S helix (S229D and F222E) or the HAMP domain (I187E) show a shallower dose–response curve, in addition to the aforementioned higher basal levels (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-di-GMP titration experimental data on mutant proteins and reference to Figure 9B.

claim: The deregulation of LapD through destabilization of regulatory interactions in the cytoplasmic domains is a result of altered sensitivity of these mutant c-di-GMP receptors.
source: These experiments establish that the deregulation of LapD through destabilization of regulatory interactions in the cytoplasmic domains is a result of altered sensitivity of these mutant c-di-GMP receptors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing altered dose-response curves for mutant proteins.

claim: Wild-type LapD exhibits switch-like behavior, which suggests cooperativity as an important regulatory feature for LapD activation.
source: These studies also reveal a switch-like behavior of the wild-type protein, which suggests cooperativity as an important regulatory feature for LapD activation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the sharp transition observed in c-di-GMP titration experiments.

claim: There is a distinct lack of penetrant phenotypes for output domain mutations tested, despite the fact that non-conservative mutations were introduced at pivotal positions.
source: Considering the group of output domain mutations tested, there is a distinct lack of penetrant phenotypes despite the fact that non-conservative mutations were introduced at pivotal positions based on the structural analysis and sequence alignments (Figure 10A, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data and reference to Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hypo-biofilm phenotypes of mutant LapD variants D72K and Y76R can be explained by disturbance of the LapG binding interface by these mutations.
source: The more apparent hypo-biofilm phenotypes of mutant LapD variants D72K and Y76R can be explained by disturbance of the LapG binding interface by these mutations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on biofilm assay data and structural knowledge of the binding interface.

claim: More than half of the single-point mutations made in the HAMP domain result in hyper-biofilm phenotypes indicative of a constitutive LapD–LapG interaction.
source: More than half of the single-point mutations made in the HAMP domain result in hyper-biofilm phenotypes indicative of a constitutive LapD–LapG interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data on HAMP domain mutants.

claim: The positions in the helical segments of the HAMP domain that are important for the differential packing interactions within the dimeric HAMP domain (positions a and d in the knobs-into-holes packing) have the most pronounced effect on LapD function.
source: Of note, the positions in the helical segments of the HAMP domain, which are important for the differential packing interactions within the dimeric HAMP domain (positions a and d in the knobs-into-holes packing; Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 2), have the most pronounced effect on LapD function.
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data and reference to Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: LapD's HAMP domain adopts a canonical fold and is likely subject to a similar mode of regulation as has been described for other HAMP domains.
source: This observation indicates that LapD's HAMP domain adopts a canonical fold and is likely subject to a similar mode of regulation as has been described for other HAMP domains.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the mutational analysis and comparison to other HAMP domain-containing proteins.

claim: The HAMP domain drives the main regulatory effects in LapD, which may be important to bias the system to inside-out signaling and to prevent accidental activation through basal LapD–LapG encounters.
source: Together, these results confirm the regulatory role of the HAMP domain, but also indicate a clear hierarchy of LapD's control elements, with the HAMP domain driving the main regulatory effects, which may be important to bias the system to inside-out signaling and to prevent accidental activation through basal LapD–LapG encounters.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the mutational analysis showing the dominance of HAMP domain effects.

claim: The majority of chimeric LapD constructs containing domains from L. pneumophila CdgS9 supported biofilm regulation similar to the levels observed with the native P. fluorescens proteins.
source: Notably, the majority of our chimeric constructs supported biofilm regulation similar to the levels observed with the native P. fluorescens proteins (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data on chimeric constructs and reference to Figure 10B.

claim: Both the output domain and the cytoplasmic HAMP-GGDEF-EAL module from L. pneumophila appeared fully functional in the context of P. fluorescens LapD.
source: Importantly, both the output domain and the cytoplasmic HAMP-GGDEF-EAL module from L. pneumophila appeared fully functional in this context.
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data on chimeric constructs.

claim: The only chimeric construct that generated a hyper-biofilm phenotype was the one in which the L. pneumophila S helix-GGDEF-EAL fragment replaced the respective P. fluorescens LapD domains with the HAMP domain coming from P. fluorescens (construct Pfl-Lpg C5).
source: The only construct that generated a hyper-biofilm phenotype indicative of a constitutive interaction between LapG and LapD was the one in which the L. pneumophila S helix-GGDEF-EAL fragment replaced the respective P. fluorescens LapD domains with the HAMP domain coming from P. fluorescens (construct Pfl-Lpg C5).
evidence: This claim is supported by biofilm assay data on chimeric constructs.

claim: The chimeric construct data hint at the importance of the connection between the HAMP domain and the S helix.
source: This result hints at the importance of the connection between the HAMP domain and the S helix.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the biofilm phenotype of the Pfl-Lpg C5 chimeric construct.

claim: The data demonstrate conservation of the key mechanism between moderately conserved LapD orthologs.
source: Most importantly for this study, these data demonstrate conservation of the key mechanism between moderately conserved LapD orthologs and indicate that, despite the mixed origin of the complex structure components, CdgS9 is a suitable proxy for a c-di-GMP receptor that mediates inside-out signaling to control periplasmic proteolysis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the functional complementation observed with chimeric constructs.

claim: LapD's output domain adopts a PAS domain fold and forms homo-dimers with distinct differences in the LapG binding-competent, active state and its inactive state.
source: Our structural analyses establish that LapD's output domain adopts a PAS domain fold and forms homo-dimers with distinct differences in the LapG binding-competent, active state and its inactive state (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and reference to Video 1.

claim: The packing transition that the structures depict can be described as a transition from a four-helix to a two-helix bundle, following two principle components: a piston motion and scissor-like motions.
source: Notably, the packing transition that the structures depict can be described as a transition from a four-helix to a two-helix bundle, and follows two principle components: in a piston motion, one half-side of the dimeric output domain shifts vertically along the second half-side, whereas scissor-like motions encompass a tilting of the half-sides along the dimer interface.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural changes observed between the apo and LapG-bound states.

claim: The output domain follows the conformational changes in the HAMP domain as a direct response.
source: Considering the current model for HAMP domain-switching (Hulko et al., 2006; Airola et al., 2013), which involves undergoing small amplitude translations and/or rotations during signal transduction similar to the ones we describe for CdgS9's periplasmic output domain, we predict that the output domain follows the conformational changes in the HAMP domain as a direct response.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on comparison to known HAMP domain switching mechanisms and the structural observations.

claim: The cross-over of the membrane proximal elements observed in both output domain conformations may function as the fulcrum about which the output and HAMP domain pivot and/or tilt.
source: The cross-over of the membrane proximal elements observed in both output domain conformations (Figure 4B) may function as the fulcrum about which the output and HAMP domain pivot and/or tilt.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on structural observations and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The four-helix bundle of the output domain of inactive LapD presents a surface that appears suboptimal for LapG binding.
source: As for the mode of LapG interaction, the four-helix bundle of the output domain of inactive LapD presents a surface that appears suboptimal for LapG binding, while the activated LapD conformation is characterized by extensive shape complementarity and effective interaction anchors at one face of the LapD output domain dimer, foremost the conserved tryptophan in the GWxQ loop.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on structural analysis of the apo and LapG-bound states.

claim: The activated LapD conformation is characterized by extensive shape complementarity and effective interaction anchors at one face of the LapD output domain dimer, foremost the conserved tryptophan in the GWxQ loop.
source: As for the mode of LapG interaction, the four-helix bundle of the output domain of inactive LapD presents a surface that appears suboptimal for LapG binding, while the activated LapD conformation is characterized by extensive shape complementarity and effective interaction anchors at one face of the LapD output domain dimer, foremost the conserved tryptophan in the GWxQ loop.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on structural analysis of the LapG-bound state.

claim: The notion of geometric compatibility, as opposed to an increase in specific per-residue interactions as a predominant driver for high-affinity LapG binding, is supported by the overall low surface conservation of LapD orthologs.
source: The notion of geometric compatibility, as opposed to an increase in specific per-residue interactions as a predominant driver for high-affinity LapG binding, is supported by the overall low surface conservation of LapD orthologs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on sequence conservation analysis and structural observations.

claim: The asymmetry of the LapD–LapG complex suggests mechanisms inherent to the output domain that counteract an activating signal and may ultimately contribute to anti-cooperativity.
source: The asymmetry of the LapD–LapG complex further suggests mechanisms inherent to the output domain that counteract an activating signal and may ultimately contribute to anti-cooperativity, which has been described for other PAS domain-containing proteins (Moore and Hendrickson, 2012).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the asymmetric complex structure and comparison to other PAS domain proteins.

claim: Transient occupation of the second LapG binding site on the dimeric output domain of LapD would release LapG at the first, high-affinity site.
source: In the current model, (transient) occupation of the second LapG binding site on the dimeric output domain of LapD would release LapG at the first, high-affinity site.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations and stoichiometry data.

claim: The regulatory HAMP and GGDEF-EAL domains would constrain the conformation of the LapD output domain to an extent that mutations are insufficient to destabilize the output domain dimer interface and/or induce the correct high-affinity LapG-binding state.
source: In the first model, the regulatory HAMP and GGDEF-EAL domains would constrain the conformation of the LapD output domain to an extent that mutations are insufficient to destabilize the output domain dimer interface and/or induce the correct high-affinity LapG-binding state.
evidence: This claim is a proposed explanation for the lack of penetrant phenotypes in output domain mutants.

claim: The apo-state may be described as a dynamic ensemble, preventing efficient LapG binding.
source: Another, non-mutually exclusive model also consistent with our data is that the apo-state may be described as a dynamic ensemble, preventing efficient LapG binding.
evidence: This claim is an alternative proposed explanation for the observed behavior of the output domain.

claim: The crystallized output domain in the absence of LapG depicts only one possible conformation of the ensemble with the mutations only having minimal effect on the activity.
source: It would follow that the crystallized output domain in the absence of LapG depicts only one possible conformation of the ensemble with the mutations only having minimal effect on the activity.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the dynamic ensemble model.

claim: LapD activation by c-di-GMP increases the affinity of LapG with the output domain following conformational changes dictated by the cytoplasmic HAMP domain.
source: LapD activation by c-di-GMP on the other hand increases the affinity of LapG with the output domain following conformational changes dictated by the cytoplasmic HAMP domain.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The dominance of the HAMP domain over the output domain in regulating LapD may bias the system towards inside-out signaling and against tenacious conformational changes induced by LapD–LapG encounters in the periplasm.
source: The dominance of the HAMP domain over the output domain in regulating LapD may bias the system towards inside-out signaling and against tenacious conformational changes induced by LapD–LapG encounters in the periplasm.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the mutational analysis showing HAMP domain dominance.

claim: The observed basal and/or transient interactions of LapG with LapD's output domain at low c-di-GMP levels may translate into low frequency conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domains, which would yield pre-activated receptors that would lock in place only when c-di-GMP levels are high.
source: At the same time, the observed basal and/or transient interactions of LapG with LapD's output domain at low c-di-GMP levels may translate into low frequency conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domains, which would yield pre-activated receptors that would lock in place only when c-di-GMP levels are high.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the observed basal LapG binding and c-di-GMP sensitivity.

claim: The mechanism would be best described as 'coincidence detection', requiring both c-di-GMP and LapG being available for LapD engagement and full activation.
source: Such a mechanism would explain how c-di-GMP has access to the EAL domain in the first place, given that the autoinhibited conformation is incompatible with c-di-GMP binding. The mechanism would be best described as 'coincidence detection', requiring both c-di-GMP and LapG being available for LapD engagement and full activation.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model for LapD activation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The HAMP domain would function as an attenuator in the inactive state, yet determine the active conformation upon c-di-GMP binding, which would prevent an immediate reversion to the autoinhibited state.
source: The HAMP domain would function as an attenuator in the inactive state, yet determine the active conformation upon c-di-GMP binding, which would prevent an immediate reversion to the autoinhibited state.
evidence: This claim is a proposed role for the HAMP domain based on the functional data.

claim: Gene deletion of the L. pneumophila LapD ortholog locus cdgS9 has no obvious phenotype.
source: Gene deletion of the L. pneumophila LapD ortholog locus cdgS9 has no obvious phenotype, yet overexpression of CdgS9 has an effect on intracellular growth of the pathogen (Levi et al., 2011), suggesting functional relevance of this ortholog.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levi et al., 2011, which provides external scholarly support.

claim: Overexpression of CdgS9 has an effect on intracellular growth of L. pneumophila, suggesting functional relevance of this ortholog.
source: Gene deletion of the L. pneumophila LapD ortholog locus cdgS9 has no obvious phenotype, yet overexpression of CdgS9 has an effect on intracellular growth of the pathogen (Levi et al., 2011), suggesting functional relevance of this ortholog.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levi et al., 2011 and represents an inference about functional relevance.

claim: Stronger functional similarities to the P. fluorescens system are apparent in more closely related bacteria such as Pseudomonas putida.
source: Stronger functional similarities to the P. fluorescens system are apparent in more closely related bacteria such as Pseudomonas putida (Gjermansen et al., 2005, 2006, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gjermansen et al., 2005, 2006, 2010, which provide external scholarly support.

claim: In principle, the LapD–LapG interaction, and likely analogous binding between similar protein pairs, is therapeutically accessible, since LapD-derived peptides containing the conserved GWxQ motif specifically diminish LapG binding to LapD.
source: As part of these efforts, we demonstrate that, in principle, the LapD–LapG interaction, and likely analogous binding between similar protein pairs, is therapeutically accessible, since LapD-derived peptides containing the conserved GWxQ motif specifically diminish LapG binding to LapD.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide competition experimental data.

claim: Effective competition relied on high peptide concentrations, which needs to be considered given that a non-constrained peptide was used.
source: While effective competition relied on high peptide concentrations, one needs to consider that we used a non-constrained peptide, which competes with the native binding site presented by full-length, c-di-GMP-activated LapD that presents an interaction surface far greater than just the peptide sequence.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the peptide competition experimental results.

claim: The peptides are not bioavailable and likely do not cross the outer membrane of P. fluorescens.
source: Unfortunately, the peptides are not bioavailable and likely do not cross the outer membrane of P. fluorescens, preventing us to assess whether inhibiting the LapD–LapG interaction would result in increased biofilm dispersal, as would be predicted if the peptides would release LapG from LapD in vivo.
evidence: This claim is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the properties of the peptides used.

claim: Targeting the interaction site with small-molecule inhibitors could be a fruitful strategy to perturb bacterial biofilm formation and dispersal.
source: Nevertheless, our data indicate that targeting the interaction site with small-molecule inhibitors could be a fruitful strategy to perturb bacterial biofilm formation and dispersal.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the peptide competition data.

claim: Optimized competitors may include synthetic stapled or otherwise designed peptides that mimic the loop structure in solution.
source: Optimized competitors may include synthetic stapled or otherwise designed peptides that mimic the loop structure in solution (Razavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about potential improvements to the peptide inhibitors, supported by a citation to Razavi et al., 2014.

claim: Based on the conservation of binding events, regulation and key sequence motifs, the model is predicted to be universal for proteins with LapD-like architecture.
source: Based on the conservation of binding events, regulation and key sequence motifs, we predict that our model is universal for proteins with LapD-like architecture, which includes receptors that signal in the opposite direction ('outside-in') by translating environmental signals emerging in the periplasm into changes in DGC and/or PDE activity in their cytoplasmic GGDEF and EAL domains, respectively.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the conservation analysis and functional studies.

claim: A LapDG-like mode of regulation, yet in the opposite signaling direction and involving an active DGC, controls the clinically important GGDEF domain-containing protein YfiN from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and E. coli.
source: As an example, a LapDG-like mode of regulation, yet in the opposite signaling direction and involving an active DGC, controls the clinically important GGDEF domain-containing protein YfiN from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and E. coli (Malone et al., 2010; Sanchez-Torres et al., 2011; Malone et al., 2012; Giardina et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Malone et al., 2010; Sanchez-Torres et al., 2011; Malone et al., 2012; Giardina et al., 2013) that provide external scholarly support.

claim: In the YfiN system, the periplasmic protein YfiR suppresses YfiN's DGC activity through a direct interaction with YfiN's periplasmic PAS domain.
source: In this case, the periplasmic protein YfiR suppresses YfiN's DGC activity through a direct interaction with YfiN's periplasmic PAS domain (Malone et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Malone et al., 2012, which provides external scholarly support.

claim: YfiR becomes sequestered by the outer membrane protein YfiB, which activates YfiN, likely involving conformational changes in its HAMP-GGDEF domain module.
source: YfiR becomes sequestered by the outer membrane protein YfiB, which activates YfiN, likely involving conformational changes in its HAMP-GGDEF domain module (Malone et al., 2012; Raterman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malone et al., 2012 and Raterman et al., 2013, which provide external scholarly support.

claim: A similar outside-in signaling model describing a rheostat-like control mechanism has been established for an autoinducing peptide-sensitive histidine kinase reconstituted into membrane nano-discs.
source: Recently, a similar outside-in signaling model describing a rheostat-like control mechanism has been established for an autoinducing peptide-sensitive histidine kinase reconstituted into membrane nano-discs (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014, which provides external scholarly support.
